clue_cards.insight: Sometimes a heavy roof just needs a tall, strong pillar in the middle to stop it from sagging downwards.

clue_cards.title: Twist and Tie
clue_cards.insight: If you poke two small holes in the cardboard, you could thread something bendy through them to tie the flaps together.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 1: Clothespin Clips
potential_solutions.description: Pinch the overlapping cardboard flaps together using the wooden clothespins to lock them firmly in place so they don't fall.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 2: Broom Pillar
potential_solutions.description: Stand the long broom handle straight up in the middle of your spaceship to prop up the sagging roof from the inside.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 3: Pipe Cleaner Ties
potential_solutions.description: Poke small holes through the roof flaps where they meet and twist the fuzzy pipe cleaners through the holes to tie the roof shut securely.

title: The Runaway Marble
complaint: Hi! I'm Jayden. I'm building a giant cardboard marble run in my living room, but every time the marble hits the bottom corner, it flies right off the track!

clue_cards.title: Clue 1: Bumper Walls
clue_cards.insight: If you build a wall out of something sticky and squishy, the marble will bump into it and stay on the path.

clue_cards.title: Clue 2: Safe Tunnels
clue_cards.insight: Sometimes the best way to keep a marble from flying away is to guide it through a round wall.

clue_cards.title: Clue 3: Speed Bumps
clue_cards.insight: If the marble is going too fast, putting something soft on the track right before the turn will slow it down.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 1: Direct Action
potential_solutions.description: Mold the modeling clay into a high, curved bumper wall on the outside edge of the corner so the marble safely bounces around the turn.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 2: Environmental Adaptation
potential_solutions.description: Place the soft sponge right on the track just before the sharp corner to act as a speed bump, slowing the marble down so it doesn't fly off.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 3: Lateral Swap
potential_solutions.description: Cut the bottom out of the paper cup and tape it sideways around the corner to create a high-walled tunnel that traps the marble and guides it down.

title: The Floppy Robot Fix
complaint: Hi! I'm Stella. I am building a giant cardboard robot for the school science fair in my bedroom workshop, but I have a big problem. The robot's cardboard arms keep flopping down, and I need them to stay up to hold a little flag, but I am completely out of glue and tape!

clue_cards.title: Clue 1: Bendy Metal
clue_cards.insight: If you poke a metal pin with bendable legs through two pieces of cardboard, you can fold the legs flat to hold the pieces together.

clue_cards.title: Clue 2: Twisty Ties
clue_cards.insight: Fuzzy wires can act like strong string. If you make holes, you can thread them through and twist them tight.

clue_cards.title: Clue 3: The Peg Method
clue_cards.insight: Sometimes sticking a long, pointy stick straight through the arm and into the body will pin it perfectly in place.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 1: Brass Fastener Joints
potential_solutions.description: Poke the brass fasteners through the robot's arms and into the body, then spread the metal legs flat on the inside to create tight, movable shoulders.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 2: Pipe Cleaner Ties
potential_solutions.description: Use a pencil to poke small holes in the arms and body, thread the pipe cleaners through the holes, and twist the fuzzy ends tightly together to tie the arms upright.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 3: Wooden Skewer Pegs
potential_solutions.description: Push the wooden skewers directly through the top of the cardboard arms and deep into the side of the robot's body to pin the arms firmly in place.

title: The Runaway Marble
complaint: Hi! I'm Gabriel. I'm building a giant cardboard marble roller coaster in my backyard, but every time the marble hits the big bottom curve, it flies right off the track into the grass!

clue_cards.title: Moldable Wall
clue_cards.insight: Sometimes you need a shape that fits perfectly around a corner. Is there something squishy you can mold into a thick barrier?

clue_cards.title: Speed Bump
clue_cards.insight: If the marble is going way too fast, maybe something soft can absorb the bump and slow it down just enough to stay on the track.

clue_cards.title: Safety Rail
clue_cards.insight: Roller coasters for humans have high walls on sharp turns. Can you bend something fuzzy to make a curved fence?

potential_solutions.title: Solution 1: Clay Bumper
potential_solutions.description: Roll the modeling clay into a thick snake and press it along the outside edge of the cardboard curve to act as a solid, sticky wall that bounces the marble back on track.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 2: Soft Slowdown
potential_solutions.description: Place the kitchen sponge right before the sharp curve. The marble will roll over it, slow down just enough from the soft surface, and safely make the turn without flying off.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 3: Bendable Guardrail
potential_solutions.description: Bend the pipe cleaner to match the shape of the sharp curve and stick it into the edges of the cardboard to make a tall, flexible guardrail that catches the marble.

title: The Runaway Marbles
complaint: Hi! I'm Isaac. I am building a giant marble run on my bedroom wall, but every time the marbles hit the sharp bottom corner, they fly right off the track and bounce under my bed!

clue_cards.title: Bumper Cars
clue_cards.insight: If the track is open, the marble will jump. Can you build a soft wall to catch it?

clue_cards.title: Tunnel Time
clue_cards.insight: If you cover the top of the track, the marble has nowhere to go but down the path.

clue_cards.title: Smooth the Turn
clue_cards.insight: Sharp turns make things crash. Is there a way to stretch out the track so the turn is gentle?

potential_solutions.title: Solution 1: Direct Action
potential_solutions.description: Squish the Play-Doh along the outside edge of the sharp corner to build a bouncy wall that catches the marbles and keeps them on the track.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 2: Environmental Adaptation
potential_solutions.description: Slide the cardboard tubes over the corner of the track to create a closed-in tunnel, stopping the marbles from flying out into the room.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 3: Lateral Swap
potential_solutions.description: Instead of blocking the marbles, use the masking tape to change the layout of the track entirely, taping it further down the wall to make the turn wider and slower.

title: The Slipping Screen
complaint: Hi! I'm Willow. I'm trying to film a stop-motion animation video for my portfolio at my crafting desk, but the cheap plastic phone tripod just snapped in half and my phone keeps sliding flat onto the table!

clue_cards.title: Pinch and Stand
clue_cards.insight: Office supplies that grip tightly can often be flipped upside down to create a surprisingly sturdy base.

clue_cards.title: Sticky Support
clue_cards.insight: Sometimes the best way to keep a device from sliding is to mold a temporary, sticky anchor right to the desk.

clue_cards.title: Heavy Wedge
clue_cards.insight: Dense objects with pages can easily act as a makeshift clamp to hold thin, flat items perfectly upright.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 1: Direct Action
potential_solutions.description: Clip a large binder clip to the bottom edge of your phone. You can rest the flat base of the clip on the table and even remove the silver arms so the phone stays perfectly propped up.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 2: Environmental Adaptation
potential_solutions.description: Roll a generous piece of poster putty into a thick log. Press it firmly against the desk and wedge your phone into it to hold the camera perfectly steady at the exact angle you need.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 3: Lateral Swap
potential_solutions.description: Take one of the heavy books, open it slightly, and wedge the bottom edge of the phone tightly between the pages. The weight of the book will keep the phone upright and stop it from slipping.

title: The Prototyping Predicament
complaint: Hi! I'm Character_57. I'm sitting at my home desk trying to build a delicate cardboard prototype for a new product idea, but I have a huge problem. I need to hold two freshly glued pieces of the cardboard tightly together while they dry, but I don't have any clamps, and regular tape will tear the top layer of the cardboard right off!

clue_cards.title: Pressure Points
clue_cards.insight: Look for small everyday items with springs that can pinch things together gently without causing damage.

clue_cards.title: Gravity is Free
clue_cards.insight: If you can't pinch the edges, think about laying the pieces flat and using plain old weight to press them together.

clue_cards.title: Gentle Adhesives
clue_cards.insight: Standard tape is too strong, but there might be common office supplies with a much weaker glue designed to be peeled off safely.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 1: Direct Action
potential_solutions.description: Use the hair clips as miniature clamps. Slide them over the edges of the glued cardboard pieces to pinch them firmly in place until the glue dries.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 2: Environmental Adaptation
potential_solutions.description: Lay the glued cardboard pieces flat on the desk and stack the heavy textbooks on top of them. The weight will press the pieces together evenly while the glue sets.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 3: Lateral Swap
potential_solutions.description: Use the sticky notes as a temporary, gentle tape. The adhesive band on the notes is strong enough to keep the cardboard pieces aligned, but weak enough to peel off later without tearing the surface.

title: The Bucket Dilemma
complaint: Hi! I'm Character_57. I'm trying to mop the floors in my new apartment, but the mop bucket is way too big to fit under the tiny bathroom sink faucet.

clue_cards.title: Bridging the Gap
clue_cards.insight: Look for an object that can act like a slide or ramp to carry the water over the edge of the sink.

clue_cards.title: Custom Plumbing
clue_cards.insight: One of your items can be easily molded and folded to create a waterproof channel.

clue_cards.title: Flexible Transport
clue_cards.insight: If you can't get the water directly from the tap to the bucket, find something waterproof to line the sink and carry the water manually.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 1: The Dustpan Ramp
potential_solutions.description: Place the wide dust-catching end of the dustpan under the faucet. The water will pool in the pan and flow out through the hollow handle, dropping straight into the bucket on the floor.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 2: Foil Trough
potential_solutions.description: Fold the heavy-duty aluminum foil several times to make a thick, sturdy V-shape. Use this custom trough to guide the running water from the faucet, over the counter edge, and into the bucket.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 3: Trash Bag Transfer
potential_solutions.description: Line the sink bowl with the thick plastic trash bag and let it fill with water from the faucet. Once it's full, gather the top of the bag securely, lift it out of the sink, and gently pour the water into the bucket.

title: The Stubborn Scroll
complaint: Hi! I'm Character_57. I am trying to map out a big project on this massive paper blueprint in my home office, but it just keeps rolling back up like a giant scroll every time I let go of the edges!

clue_cards.title: Weighty Matters
clue_cards.insight: Sometimes the simplest way to stop something from moving is to put something heavy on top of it.

clue_cards.title: Shift Your Perspective
clue_cards.insight: If the desk isn't working for you, see if you can use a different surface entirely, like a wall.

clue_cards.title: Reverse the Memory
clue_cards.insight: Paper tends to hold its shape. Bending it the opposite way around a solid cylinder can help cancel out the curl.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 1: Direct Action
potential_solutions.description: Place the heavy ceramic coffee mug on the most stubborn corner of the blueprint to weigh it down and keep it flat on your desk.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 2: Environmental Adaptation
potential_solutions.description: Use the roll of painter's tape to stick the blueprint directly onto an empty wall, letting gravity help keep the paper flat and unrolled.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 3: Lateral Swap
potential_solutions.description: Carefully wrap the blueprint around the cardboard mailing tube in the opposite direction of its natural curl to flatten out the paper.

title: The Flapping Screen
complaint: Hi! I'm Character_57. I'm setting up a backyard movie night with a white bedsheet draped over my clothesline, but every time a slight breeze rolls through, the sheet violently flaps around and slides right off the wire!

clue_cards.title: Clue 1: Pinch Points
clue_cards.insight: Securing the top edge tightly to the line with a strong grip will prevent it from slipping off sideways.

clue_cards.title: Clue 2: Bottom Heavy
clue_cards.insight: Adding dead weight to the bottom edge of the sheet will stop it from catching the wind like a sail.

clue_cards.title: Clue 3: Tension is Key
clue_cards.insight: Pulling the bottom corners down and anchoring them to a fixed point nearby will keep the screen perfectly flat.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 1: Direct Action
potential_solutions.description: Use the large binder clips to firmly pinch the top edge of the bedsheet directly to the clothesline, stopping it from sliding off when the wind blows.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 2: Environmental Adaptation
potential_solutions.description: Gather the bottom corners of the sheet and tie the heavy metal washers into the fabric to act as anchors, keeping the sheet hanging straight down.

potential_solutions.title: Solution 3: Lateral Swap
potential_solutions.description: Hook one end of the bungee cords to the bottom corners of the sheet and stretch the other end to the base of the clothesline poles to pull the screen tight and flat.
